I consulted lawyers, but mostly I thought about it myself, because it's my profession and my long professional career to investigate and to collect evidence. I decided not to do anything about it, knowing that the time would come for me to say what I know about this. That's why I was rather inclined to come here once I was invited to appear before the Court and say this. Let me conclude by saying that as a human being and as a professional, I would honestly like to know how my name found its way into this document. I stress once again that on this matter I know absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Three quick follow-up questions on that, sir. All yes-or-no questions. You don't contest that there was a mass grave at Tomasica, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILE MATIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can ask, yes. I found out later that there was a grave. I don't know what size, but I know it exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You don't contest that it was covered up, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILE MATIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How long it remained unfound testifies to the fact that it was covered up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You say by virtue of your position and rank, you weren't able to be involved in that. In fact, you were able to be involved in whatever tasks were assigned to you by your superiors; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MATIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At the moment, speaking in principle, you say by virtue of your position and rank, you weren't able to be involved in this. If a superior had ordered you to be involved, you'd have been able to be involved; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MATIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have inspired me now, although I have been thinking about this before. Looking at the composition of this meeting, you see Bogojevic, Colonel Arsic, Mr. Drljaca, and General Subotic. Yes, he is here as a representative of Republika Srpska before the president of the republic. All these men are at a level which is far beyond my powers. I have long thought about this list. If there were to be a representative of the MUP at such a meeting, it would be something -- someone of a higher level, above mine. If I had been assigned to go to that meeting, however, I would have gone and later I would have acted as planned. But I really don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No further questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. May I just seek clarification. Is it -- the witness said "looking at the composition of this meeting," you haven't asked him any questions about the composition of the meeting, did you? So, therefore, I do not know what the position of the Prosecution is. Is it the position of the Prosecution that this witness was present at this meeting, which does not immediately transpire for me, or is it the position of the Prosecution that what is recorded here is what Colonel Bogojevic told about a team who would deal with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have -- sorry, I've lost the page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was page 154 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- or would it be 151 which would be perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the page in which the meeting is announced as --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We've got the right page in e-court now. I think it's English page 155 and B/C/S 159. And so there are two meetings at issue. The first is the meeting at which General Mladic is taking notes. It is not our position that Mr. Matijevic attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Colonel Bogojevic is here -- I'm slowing down for the transcript. Is here recorded as reporting to General Mladic about a team but also about a meeting. He says: "At the meeting were General Subotic, Arsic, Drljaca, and Mile Matijevic." And our position is that we rely on the notebook entry for its truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to have matters perfectly clear, that it's the position of the Prosecution not that you attended the meeting with Mr. Mladic but that what is written by Mr. Mladic, that reference is made to a meeting and it's the position of the Prosecution that you were present at that meeting. And I do understand that you say: I never have been at such a meeting where General Subotic, Mr. Arsic, Mr. Drljaca were present. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it has been cleared up accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, after all this clarification, the Defence has no further questions for this witness. I thank the witness on behalf of the Defence team of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one short question for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your statement, you describe how Mr. Drljaca was -- was not really acting in accordance with the rules, if I could say so. He was acting on his own, not consulting those he would have to had consulted. Was that feasible for you at all that someone would not act in accordance with the rules?

utterances.speaker: MILE MATIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I emphasised earlier and it was commonly known that Mr. Drljaca, as the head of the public security station and later as chief of centre, acted rather autonomously, and he was more associated to the Crisis Staff than the police centre and the Ministry of Interior. Why he acted in that way is not for me to tell. But I believe that as a senior person from the SDS, he was simply more susceptible or perhaps more aware that it was necessary to have stronger links with the Crisis Staff than with the organisational units of the Ministry of Interior. For that reason, it sometimes happened that he would report rather to the one than to the other, and he would even make decisions without prior consent from the Ministry of Interior. We have discussed this earlier today. He even had to bear some consequences of his actions later. He was moved to different positions, and they were not all promotions, as the Prosecutor hinted. There were shifts but not necessarily prosecutions -- promotions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which one was not a promotion? Which one was a -- where he was removed and brought to a lower position? Because we have heard a few examples mentioned by the Prosecution. If you say it were not all promotions, could you tell us of any occasion where he was not promoted but rather degraded? Or left at the same level which ...

utterances.speaker: MILE MATIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just commenting upon the earlier statement of the Prosecutor that he kept moving up. However, when I said shifts from one position to another, it means that you are sometimes not doing your work up to snuff. I have to admit, however, that Mr. Drljaca wielded great authority among the civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understood that, but I was asking for an example of that. Because you say -- you commented on a position taken by the Prosecution. I understand that not necessarily how you consider it had been. Now, could you then give us an example of a switch or a shift where it was not a promotion?

utterances.speaker: MILE MATIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by the facts we have at our disposal that he was moved to some higher positions, that is not in accordance with my interpretation. But if I may say so, I had this feeling, as I knew Mr. Drljaca, that when he left for the MUP, he certainly accepted that he didn't agree at some point. People did not eagerly leave their posts when they were moved or shifted to other organisational units away from their places of residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm asking you for a shift which you could not reasonably understand as being a promotion, an example of that.

utterances.speaker: MILE MATIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of Mr. Drljaca, all the posts which he was assigned later were at higher levels than the chief of station where he started from, so we couldn't say that he was demoted. But sometimes people would not accept being shifted to higher-ranking positions, if I may say that. I did not agree to be sent to Bijeljina because I had to leave my family and go to a different town, but that was the requirement of service at the time. So I did not see it as any sort of special promotion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I then understand that the fact - and I'm moving away now from promotion or not - the fact that the rules prescribe how to act and whom to consult and whom to report to, that those rules do not necessarily involve that that is how one acted with Mr. Drljaca as an example of that?

utterances.speaker: MILE MATIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really -- if you could clarify that a little bit in terms of what the substance or the gist is. In terms of how one acts or what the rules are? I do not really understand the substance of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you say Mr. Drljaca was not fulfilling his duties in accordance with the rules but, rather, reported to, for example, party organs, SDS. And my question is: Does this mean that even if there are rules which prescribe to whom to report and to whom to consult, et cetera, that this does not necessarily mean that that is what was done in practice?

utterances.speaker: MILE MATIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That's just how it could be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Traldi:

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, just to make sure I understood a portion of your prior testimony correctly, you have no direct personal knowledge of who Mr. Drljaca reported to or consulted with during the period between May and August of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE MATIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period between May and August, I did not discharge a regional duty so I was not informed about his duties or his communications. I only knew him by sight when I was at the Banja Luka police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's all I had, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further. Mr. Matijevic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your co-operation, and my greetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have a few items on our agenda, a few decisions to be read, which I'd like to do now, and with a bit of luck we'll be able to finish that before we have to take another break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I first like to add a few words to what we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday I indicated that the court sessions for the purpose of hearing evidence during the second, the third, and the fourth week of February are cancelled. Not every session but at least for sessions to hear evidence. The reason for this is that it has not been possible to schedule witnesses for that period. The Chamber therefore expects the parties to spend this time preparing for the next phases of the case, in particular, the rebuttal case and preparation of their final briefs. When later setting a date for the submission of the final briefs, the Chamber will consider these non-sitting periods against the overall time for the parties' preparation of the briefs. In this respect, the Chamber seeks to minimise the negative effect the problematic witness scheduling could have on the overall scheduling of the case. Then I'll move on. First delivering a decision. The Chamber will deliver its decision on the admission of P7527. During the testimony of Simo Tusevljak on the 1st of September of last year, an Official Note from an interview by the Agency for Investigation and Documentation in Sarajevo was marked for identification as P7527 pending the provision of a complete English translation. On the 3rd of September, the Prosecution advised the Chamber and the Defence via e-mail that the translation had been uploaded under doc ID 0105-8653-1-ET. Following further discussion in court on the 22nd of October, the Defence made additional submissions in court on the 27th of October objecting to its admission by challenging the document's authenticity. The Defence submitted that the Official Note is not addressed to a recipient, there's not any information about its author, and the case and protocol numbers are not specified. Further, the interview referred to is not attached to the report. The Prosecution was invited to make submissions by the 29th of October. On that day, the Prosecution submitted that the format of the Official Note was customary, meaning that the absence of the various items highlighted by the Defence was standard. The Defence responded by pointing out that the name of the official creating the note was not printed and that the signature cannot be deciphered. The applicable law governing the admission of evidence is set out in the Rule 89(C) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which allows a Chamber to admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. While authenticity is a factor for consideration in determining the probative value of tendered evidence, definitive proof of reliability is not required. Prima facie evidence of reliability on the basis of sufficient indicia is sufficient to grant the admission of tendered evidence. The Chamber has reviewed P7527 in light of the parties' submissions and finds that the Defence's objections relate to the weight the Chamber might attach to it rather than to its admissibility. The Chamber notes in this respect the following: The content of the Official Note, the document upon which the Defence focussed its objections to the admission of P7527, shows consistency with the other documents contained therein, namely, the death certificate and the medical report on cause of death. The latter two documents bear signatures, and P7527 was received by the Prosecution from the Agency for Research and Investigation in Sarajevo. The Chamber finds that there are sufficient indicia for prima facie proof of reliability and that P7527 is relevant and has probative value pursuant to Rule 89(C) of the Rules. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach the complete English translation to P7527 and admits the document into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. I move on to the next decision to be read out, which is the Chamber's decision on the admission of a document marked for identification as P7608 during the testimony of Mile Poparic. The Defence objected to the admission of the document into evidence, submitting that the document's author is not identified and that it is unclear whether the document was dated contemporaneously. To be found on transcript pages 40731 through -732. On the 5th of November, 2015, the Prosecution advised the Chamber that the document was manifestly prepared by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina for contemporaneous reporting purposes through the intelligence chain and is not dissimilar in content to Exhibit P7609. To be found at page 40950. The Defence argued that the document does not state that it was prepared by the army and reiterated that the document's author is not identified. And that's to be found on the page following the one I previously referred to. The Chamber recalls that the applicable law for the admission of evidence is set out in Rule 89(C) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence which allows a Chamber to admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. With regard to relevance, the Chamber finds that the document, which deals, inter alia, with VRS firing positions and weaponry at the theology building, relates to the charges in the Sarajevo component of the case. The Chamber also notes that the Defence does not challenge the document's relevance. With regard to the Defence's objection that the author of the document is not identified, the Chamber notes the signed attestation of Captain Ragib Podrug - that is P7608, page 3 in e-court - confirming that the document is a true copy of the original filed in the archives of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In light of this, the Chamber considers that although it's not entirely clear who created the document, this is a matter which goes to the weight, if any, to be attached to the document as opposed to its admission. This also applies to the Defence's objection concerning the date of the document. For the foregoing reasons, the Chamber finds that the document is relevant and of probative value and admits P7608 into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Then I move to another decision which is a decision on the admission of Mile Dosenovic's expert report. On 13th of August, 2015, the Chamber marked the expert report of Mile Dosenovic for identification as D1187 under seal. The same day, the Chamber invited the parties to file further submissions regarding report -- the report's admission into evidence. To be found at transcript pages 37744 and -45. On the 30th of October, 2015, the Prosecution notified the Chamber and the Defence via an e-mail that it had no objection to the report's admission. With respect to the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber recalls the applicable law governing the admission of evidence set out in Rules 89(C) and 94 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and refers to its decision of the 19th of October, 2012, concerning expert witness Richard Butler. The Chamber also recalls its oral decision of the 22nd of May on Dosenovic's expertise and considers that the content of his expert report, which is in the field of radio communications and intercepts, falls within the scope of his stated expertise and specialised knowledge, namely, in the area of military communication systems. The report is relevant to a number of documents admitted in this case. The Chamber finds that the report may assist the Chamber in understanding issues such as those related to intercepted communications between VRS units. The Chamber notes that the report was presented by an expert witness and it was consistent with witness's specialised knowledge and skills. It further considers the report to have probative value for the purposes of its admission into evidence. Accordingly, the Chamber finds that Dosenovic's expert report meets the standard of admission and, pursuant to Rule 89(C) and 94 bis, admits D1187 into evidence under seal. I now move to a remaining issue from the testimony of Witness Dusan Pavlovic. The Chamber hereby confirms the confidential status of P7792, which was marked for identification on the 2nd of February, 2016, and instructs the Registry that it should remain under seal. I move to remaining issue from the testimony of Ostoja Marjanovic. On the 11th of December, 2015, the Prosecution advised the Chamber and the Defence via an e-mail that it sought admission of document bearing Rule 65 ter 33385a, which is the audio and accompanying transcript of Witness Ostoja Marjanovic's prior interview with the Prosecution. This was played to the witness at transcript pages 40996 and -997. As it was read into the record, the Chamber does not require the interview excerpt to be in evidence separately. A remaining issue now from the testimony of Savo Strbac. During the testimony of Savo Strbac on the 10th of November, 2015, P7638 was reserved for an excerpt of a transcript of an interview with Milan Martic to be uploaded by the Prosecution. The Prosecution has uploaded the excerpt into e-court. The Chamber instructs the Registry to assign P7638 to Rule 65 ter 06754a. And the Defence has one week to revisit the matter. Next item in relation to the same witness. During the testimony Mr. Strbac on the 11th of November, 2015, Exhibit P7645, an excerpt of the witness's testimony in the Hadzic case, was admitted into evidence. That's found at transcript page 41145. On the 19th of January, the Prosecution advised that an excerpt of the exhibit had been uploaded into e-court under Rule 65 ter 33410a. The Chamber instructs the Registry to replace Exhibit P7645 with the excerpt. The Defence has one week to revisit the matter. I move to items remaining from the testimony of Witness Mitar Kovac. On the 10th of December, 2015, Exhibit D557, an excerpt of the Islamic Declaration, was admitted into evidence. Transcript page 42550 to -551. On the 11th of December, the Chamber informed the Defence and the Prosecution via an e-mail that an English translation of the document was not available. On the 23rd of December, the Prosecution advised - again via e-mail - that a new excerpt including a number of additional portions not included in the Defence excerpt and its English translation had been uploaded into e-court under Rule 65 ter 33596. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace Exhibit D557 with the revised version and gives the Defence one week to revisit the matter. Next is about D1358, which is an extract from a manual on the Law of Land Warfare, which on the 16th of November, 2015, was marked for identification pending the provision of a B/C/S translation and an agreement between the parties on the extract to be tendered. Transcript page 41382 to -383. On the 18th of November, the Defence informed the Chamber and the Prosecution via e-mail that the whole manual had been uploaded into e-court under Rule 65 ter 1D00456a. On the 26th of November, the Chamber e-mailed the Defence and the Prosecution, reminding them of the Chamber's general guidance on the length of associated exhibits and requesting the parties to agree upon an extract to be tendered into evidence and to upload it into e-court together with its translation. The Chamber's instruction is hereby placed on the record. And the Chamber wonders whether the parties are in a position to update the Chamber on their progress in this matter. If not immediately -- perhaps you are, then we will hear from you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall inform you about this very quickly, Your Honour. I think that we are drawing it to a close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since we will not sit for some three weeks, perhaps if any in-between agreement has been reached, the Chamber would like to be informed about it already so that we don't have to remind you again after three weeks that we had had no response. Then we'll later put it on the record formally. Then I move on to a remaining issue from the testimony of Vojo Kupresanin. On the 11th of December, 2014, Exhibit P6994, a 77-page transcript of a Prosecution interview with Kupresanin, was admitted into evidence. That day, the Prosecution indicated that it would upload a version containing only the excerpts used with the witness in court. Transcript page 29686. On the 11th of December, 2015, the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence, advising that a reduced version had been uploaded under Rule 65 ter 31770a. And the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the exhibit with the newly uploaded version and gives the Defence one week to revisit the matter. I move on to a remaining issue from the testimony of Goran Krcmar. On the 26th of February, 2015, during the testimony of Krcmar, D918, an ICMP report, was marked for identification pending the provision of an English translation. The Chamber understood from subsequent e-mail correspondence that the Defence expected to receive the original English report from the ICMP the following May. On the 8th of October, the Chamber addressed the matter in court and set a deadline of 15th of October. As of today's date, the Defence has not provided an update. The Chamber once again requests an update from the Defence and sets a deadline of one week from today, and the Defence may inform the Chamber to start with by e-mail, which will then later be dealt with in court. Next item deals with miscellaneous exhibits admitted into evidence and placed provisionally under seal. Exhibits P7651, P7652, P7751, P7786, P7724, P7462, P5090, and D1288 were all admitted into evidence and placed provisionally under seal. On the 12th of January of this year, the Chamber e-mailed the parties to invite them to communicate with the Republic of Serbia to see whether it intends to file a Rule 54 bis motion in relation to these documents. The Chamber instructs the Registry to lift the confidentiality of these exhibits within six weeks of today's date, unless the Republic of Serbia files a motion to keep these documents confidential during that time. And when I said to lift the confidentiality of these exhibits within six weeks, of course, I meant to say in six weeks from now, with the same caveat. Next one is about Exhibit P2365, English translation replacement. This exhibit, Basara's handwritten history of the 6th Krajina Brigade, was admitted into evidence on the 10th of December, 2013. The Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence on the 13th of January, 2016, advising that a second revised English translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0047-8672-1 ET. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the English translation of Exhibit P2365 with the revised one and gives the Defence one week to revisit the matter, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have reached a moment where we usually take a break, that is, after one hour. We can do two things. We could continue. I can tell you that I have some five one and a half -- two and a half pages further to read. We can continue and then conclude for the day, adjourn for the day and for the next three weeks, or we can take a break now and we would --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, excuse me, I also wanted to note that I had a matter which I wish to raise that might take as long as five minutes. I hope not that much, but perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My estimate is that I would need another 15 to -- close to 20 minutes. If it's five minutes, that would mean that we would stop at 25 minutes to 2.00 and then adjourn for three weeks. Otherwise, we take a break now. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have consulted with General Mladic. He suggests that we do not take the break but continue and then finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I'll try to resist the temptation to start reading more quickly. I'll try to keep the same pace. Next one, correction in relation to Exhibit P7015, which is an SDS document and was admitted into evidence on the 22nd of October, 2015. The Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence on the 13th of January, 2016, advising that a corrected version of the excerpt had been uploaded into e-court under Rule 65 ter 06616b. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace Exhibit P7015 with the corrected version and gives the Defence one week to revisit the matter, if necessary. Next item, Exhibit P3030, a JNA report, was admitted into evidence on the 5th of December, 2013. The Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence on the 13th of January of this year, advising that a revised English translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID SA03-7203-2-ET. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the English translation of Exhibit P3030 with the revised one and gives the Defence one week to revisit the matter, if necessary. Next, Exhibit P2460, an exhibit which contains three video stills and was admitted into evidence on the 18th of September, 2013. On the 2nd of June of last year, the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence, advising that the three video stills were admitted in error and that the Prosecution should have tendered document bearing Rule 65 ter 10275c. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the exhibit with the correct document and gives the Defence one week to revisit the matter, if necessary. Next is a remaining issue from the testimony of GRM097. On the 21st of October, 2015, Exhibit P7583 was reserved for document bearing Rule 65 ter 33313, pending the provision of a DVD of the video-clip from 1 minute, 6 seconds, to 3 minutes, 5 seconds. To be found at transcript page 40141. On the 3rd of December, the Prosecution provided the Chamber, the Registry, and the Defence with the DVD. The Chamber hereby admits P7583 into evidence and gives the Defence one week to revisit the matter, if necessary. Next item deals with document P7746 tendered through Milos Kovic. On the 1st of December, 2015, excerpts of Rule 65 ter 06009 were shown to Witness Milos Kovic and were marked for identification as P7746. On the 22nd of December, the Chamber invited the Prosecution, via an e-mail, to select excerpts of the document that had been used with, inter alia, Witness Kovic. On the 13th of January, 2016, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the Defence via e-mail that the excerpts had been uploaded into e-court under Rule 65 ter 06009a. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to assign P7746 to Rule 65 ter 06009a and admits it into evidence. The Defence has one week to revisit the matter, if necessary. Some remaining issues from the testimony of Mile Poparic will now follow. I start with P7594. This document, a summary of persons killed and injured due to sniping, was admitted into evidence on the 2nd of November, 2015. The English translation did not correspond with the B/C/S original. On the 23rd of December, the Chamber invited the Prosecution via e-mail to upload a complete English translation. The Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence on the 11th of January, 2016, advising that the complete English translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID P07594 ET. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the English translation of Exhibit P7594 with the revised translation and gives the Defence one week to revisit the matter, if necessary. I move to D1326 and D1327. During Mile Poparic's testimony on the 27th of October, 2015, Exhibit Numbers D1326 and D1327 were reserved for two still images of a tracer. To be found on transcript pages 40375 and 40379. This all pending their upload into e-court. On the 30th of November, the Chamber reminded the Defence via e-mail to upload the still images into e-court. The Defence e-mailed the Chamber and the Prosecution on the 11th of December, advising that the two stills had been uploaded under Rule 65 ter 1D05932 and 1D05935. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to assign D1326 to Rule 65 ter 1D05932, and D1327 to Rule 65 ter 1D05935, and admits both into evidence. The Prosecution has one week to revisit the matter, if necessary. I move to D1332. On the 28th of October, 2015, the Chamber admitted Exhibit D1332, pages 3136 through 3139 of Nafa Taric's testimony in the Galic case, into evidence. On the 30th of November, the Chamber instructed the Defence via e-mail to upload this excerpt into e-court. The Defence e-mailed the Chamber and the Prosecution on the 10th of December, advising that the excerpt had been uploaded under Rule 65 ter 1D05744a. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to assign this 65 ter number to Exhibit D1332. I move to 1334. This exhibit, an eight-minute video recording, was admitted into evidence on the 28th of October, 2015. Transcript pages 40509 and 40959. On the 3rd of December, the Chamber instructed the Defence to inform the Chamber by 10.00 a.m. on the 7th of December whether or not it wants to rely on the dialogue contained in the video. The Defence e-mailed the Chamber and the Prosecution on the 9th of December, advising that it will be relying on video and not audio. The Defence further advise the Chamber that the times it will require are: 3 minutes, 29 seconds, to 3 minutes, 36 seconds; and 6 minutes, 26 seconds, to 6 minutes, 38 seconds. And the Chamber understands this to mean that the Defence only tenders this part of the eight-minute video. The Chamber therefore puts it on the record that only these portions of the video are admitted into evidence as D1334. Exceptionally, the Chamber will not ask the Defence to provide a new DVD containing only this excerpt. And this concludes the agenda items I had on my list for today. I stayed well within the time estimate, so it must have been a wrong estimate. Mr. Tieger, you wanted to raise a matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, this is in respect of Mr. Stojanovic's earlier comments about the 92 ter motions and I was seeking some clarification. Mr. Stojanovic mentioned that: "After consultations with my colleagues from the team -- that, by the way, was, I believe, a reference to his comment earlier in the day that "we are simply waiting to hear from Mr. Lukic who had some obligations" in order to respond to the Court's inquiry. And then Mr. Stojanovic went on: "I just wish to inform you officially for the record that, as far as we are aware, we have no further motions regarding witnesses under 92 ter. But if we have something, overlooked something, you may consider that we have no further motions for hearing witnesses under 92 ter." Now, the -- we understood that in light of the Trial Chamber's inquiry both yesterday and earlier today, earlier today the Court asked: "Because yesterday the Defence confirmed that the list of its remaining witnesses which I read out in private session is correct. The Chamber then asked the Defence to confirm its intention to withdraw all remaining Rule 92 ter motions related to witnesses not on that list, and the Chamber is seeking confirmation by the Defence ... that these remaining motions are withdrawn ..." So I simply wanted to indicate that our understanding in light of that inquiry of Mr. Stojanovic's remarks to the Trial Chamber was that after consultation with Mr. Lukic in respect of the Trial Chamber's request to the Defence to confirm its intention to withdraw all 92 ter motions for persons not on the list of remaining witnesses, which was read out yesterday in private session, that Mr. Stojanovic indeed confirmed that this was the case, although he did so in a way that indicated -- that -- apparently that any other 92 ter motions other than those that might apply to persons on the list of remaining witnesses were -- were no longer operative. He used the word "withdraw" but that's -- I wanted to make clear that that's how we understood it, to be sure that that is indeed the case, so there's no misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, in view of what Mr. Stojanovic said, I didn't yet make the effort to find out because I don't have all the many, many 92 ter motions and there was one remaining. I relied in this respect, as we often do, on our staff, that apparently there may have been some, but it was of no concern. Because if there was any remaining at all, that it was by mistake that they were not yet withdrawn. So I thought we would verify that after this court session, but since Mr. Tieger is now specifically seeking clarification, Mr. Stojanovic, could you remove his concerns?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. If there are any such 92 ter motions, not counting on the witnesses that you listed yesterday during closed session, we withdraw all those motions. I hope that I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing for us now to verify is whether there are any, and to see who was most accurate. We'll -- this being clarified, any other matter? Because if I say we're not sitting for three weeks, that is not entirely true because we are sitting on the -- if I'm not mistaken, on the 16th of February. Let me just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, we adjourn for the day, and we'll resume on the 16th of February -- no, it was the 10th. It was the 10th. I was -- if I'm not mistaken. Let me just check. There was a hearing scheduled for special purposes and that was on the -- I think it was on the 10th of February, but it could be the ... let me just check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until the 16th of February, 9.30 in the morning, when we have a special hearing. We stand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this same courtroom, I. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of February, 2016, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.31 p.m.,
